overview.headline: Voting rights law that banned literacy tests and added federal oversight

keyPoints.point: Students learn that African Americans in the South faced poll taxes, literacy tests and other restrictions when trying to vote.
keyPoints.quote: African Americans in the South faced tremendous obstacles to voting, including poll taxes, literacy tests, and other bureaucratic restrictions

keyPoints.point: Students learn that peaceful marchers in Selma gained national attention that helped push Congress to pass voting legislation.
keyPoints.quote: the attack by white state troopers on peaceful marchers in Selma, Alabama, gained national attention

keyPoints.point: Students learn that Section 2 created a nationwide prohibition on denying the vote on account of race or color.
keyPoints.quote: applied a nationwide prohibition of the denial or abridgment of the right to vote on account of race or color.

keyPoints.point: Students learn that a quarter of a million new Black voters were registered by the end of 1965 with help from federal examiners.
keyPoints.quote: By the end of 1965, a quarter of a million new Black voters had been registered, one-third by federal examiners.

keyTerms.gloss: Taxes charged before voting that made registration harder for Black citizens
keyTerms.quote: including poll taxes, literacy tests, and other bureaucratic restrictions to deny them the right to vote.

keyTerms.gloss: Reading tests used to deny registration to qualified citizens seeking to vote

keyTerms.gloss: Federal officials with power to register qualified citizens in covered places
keyTerms.quote: provided for the appointment of federal examiners (with the power to register qualified citizens to vote)
